title: Attention coldstart & warmup benchmark journal
content:
Purpose:
This is an experimental journal capturing a series of microbenchmarks and system traces aimed at understanding coldstart and short-lived-warmup behavior for attention kernels used in our serving runtime. Focus is on FlashAttention variants, paged-attention flow (KV paging), and fused-op kernels under realistic request patterns (bursty small sequences, mixed-length chat). Goal is to identify which kernel choices or scheduler heuristics cause the worst tail latency during the first 1–30 seconds after idle, and produce concrete mitigations (prefetching, tiny-batch coalescing, kernel pinning).

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Coldstart penalty is dominated by two orthogonal factors: GPU kernel JIT/initialization and device memory fragmentation + allocator path (particularly when KV paging triggers allocation of pinned staging buffers).
- FlashAttention shows superior steady-state throughput but variable first-token latency under tiny-batch (N<=4) bursts due to kernel selection overhead and micro-tuning fallback.
- Paged-attention (our KV-paging prototype) reduces memory pressure for long-context traces but increases 95–99.9th tail on coldstart because of synchronous page pulls and CPU-gpu roundtrips on miss.
- Fused ops (multi-op kernels that combine QKV, linear, and bias) are helpful for steady-state micro-benchmarks but lead to flaky cold path latency when the operator cache invalidates (e.g., after small changes to sequence length or dtype).
- Immediate mitigations implemented and validated in lab: background kernel "warmup" job on node join, async page prefetch on route detection, and a tiny-batch coalescer that holds requests up to 2ms to increase batch N for first-token. These reduce P50 cold first-token from ~95ms to ~28ms in our toy workload.

Experimental setup (how to reproduce):
- Hardware: A40 (driver 525.xx), V100 (for historical comparatives), and one p4d-style machine (placeholder) where kernel behavior differs.
- Runtime: branch warmup-experiments-2025 (github PR above). Build with CUDA 12.1 and cuBLAS/cuDNN as standard. FlashAttention v2 code path compiled with and without kernel autotuner.
- Workloads: 3 canonical traces:
  1) Chat-burst: 10 clients sending 1–2 messages each; seq lengths 32–256; inter-arrival 0–50ms (bursty).
  2) Longstream startup: single client sends a 4k-token generation that requires KV paging after 512 tokens.
  3) Tiny-infer: high QPS of small single-token queries (N<=2), used to cause tiny-batch regime.
- Tools: nvprof/nvtrace for kernel timelines, custom kernel-selection logging, allocator debug hooks (tracking tensor allocation stacks), perf for CPU threads coordinating transfers.
- Measurement window: 60s after idle; repeat 20 runs per config to compute stable tails.

Key observations (detailed):
1) Kernel selection jitter:
- When server receives the first request after a sustained idle (>30s), the runtime often invokes the kernel autotuner to pick fused vs unfused kernel or to select tiling. Tuner runs 3–6 micro-benchmarks per candidate which cost 5–40ms each depending on batch shape. On small-batch first requests this becomes the dominant contributor to the first-token latency.
- Mitigation attempted: cache tuner results by shape-signature and persist quick-checksum across restarts. This reduced autotune occurrences by ~85% across runs.

2) Allocator & pinned staging cost:
- Observed synchronous cudaHostAlloc/cudaMemcpy in the cold path when paging is enabled. On page-miss the paging code allocates pinned host buffers for stage-in; driver overhead plus TLB warmup contributes ~12–20ms on A40.
- We found that malloc fragmentation on device when previous workloads left many small tensors leads to allocator slow paths that spike the first allocation by 10–25ms. Calling cuMemAddressReserve or pre-reserving a slab at pool-init improves this.

3) KV page miss sync latency:
- Paged-attention introduces explicit CPU->GPU synchronization to copy in missing KV tiles before attention compute. Under coldstart, the async page queue worker thread is not yet warmed so the first page pull is performed on-demand synchronously, adding 15–50ms depending on tile size.
- Mitigation: weakly consistent async prefetch triggered by route hints (e.g., model + user session indicates likely long context). Also introduced early worker warmup at model load completion.

4) Fused op cache invalidation:
- Our fused operator binary cache uses a key that includes seq-length bin and dtype. We discovered a surprising invalidation when requests arrive with token-type metadata differences (e.g., presence/absence of padding mask). This causes a compile/registration step that adds 20–60ms on first use.
- Fix: normalize op keys to canonical forms and delay registration off the "hot path" (spawn background registrations for near-future bins).

Microbenchmark table (selected numbers, median / p95 first-token latency after 30s idle, A40):
- Baseline (no mitigations): FlashAttention (autotune on): P50 95ms, P95 210ms.
- Baseline: FlashAttention (autotune cached): P50 70ms, P95 120ms.
- Paged-attention enabled (no prefetch): P50 115ms, P95 310ms.
- Paged-attention + async prefetch: P50 44ms, P95 90ms.
- Fused-ops naive registration: P50 140ms, P95 420ms.
- Fused-ops + deferred registration + cache persist: P50 52ms, P95 110ms.
- Combined mitigations (cache autotune + prefetch + deferred reg + slab reserve): P50 28ms, P95 64ms, P99 115ms.

Tracer snippets (representative timeline):
- 0.0ms: request received on CPU thread T1
- 0.6ms: deserialize / tokenization
- 2.1ms: scheduler decides model shard, route to GPU A (initial warmup)
- 3.5ms: kernel autotune microbench run 1 (4ms)
- 8.1ms: cudaMalloc -> slow allocator path (13ms)
- 23.6ms: page pull (sync) for KV tile (18ms)
- 42.1ms: fused-op registration/compile (28ms)
- 70.5ms: first-token emitted

Notes on measurement noise and reproducibility: 
- Driver/OS noise: we observed spikes that correlate with concurrent agent processes on the node (e.g., checkpoint writer). For reproducible numbers we pinned experiments to isolated NUMA and disabled background cron jobs.
- Cross-GPU variance: p4d machines with A100s show similar autotune overhead but less host staging cost due to faster NVLink transfers. V100 shows higher registration times and sometimes falls back to unfused kernels.
- Repeatability: runs after applying the mitigations show much fewer tails; still saw rare >200ms events when a concurrent background GC triggered and paused the async prefetch worker for ~40ms.

Hypotheses tested (and results):
H1: Kernel autotune during first request is the main cause of first-token tail. RESULT: True. Caching + persisting reduces autotune frequency and lowers tails.
H2: Paged attention always worsens cold latency due to page pulls. RESULT: Partially true. On miss-heavy startup it does; with async prefetch and warmed prefetch workers it becomes net-positive for memory-limited workloads.
H3: Fused ops help steady-state but harm cold paths due to registration cost. RESULT: True. Deferred registration recovers the advantage without adding cold latency.

Implemented mitigations (summary):
1) Autotune cache persist: dump autotuner cache to per-model shard metadata and reload on node start.
2) Background kernel warmup worker: after model load, spin a low-priority worker that executes a representative set of shapes for a few seconds (controlled budget).
3) Async KV prefetch + route hints: when route receives a request that is likely to expand context, schedule prefetches for next few tiles.
4) Slab pre-reserve allocator: reserve a small contiguous pool on init and satisfy first allocations from it to avoid slow allocator paths.
5) Deferred fused-op registration: register binary kernels asynchronously after the first request is acknowledged to the client (i.e., trickle in registration while serving).
6) Tiny-batch coalescer (2ms hold): increase first-batch size slightly to amortize autotune and kernel overhead. Choice made configurable per model/service.

Validation runs (post-mitigations):
- Method: run Chat-burst trace 50 times with ephemeral nodes to ensure warmup sequences are measured.
- Results: Combined mitigations reduced median cold first-token latency from 95ms -> 28ms and P95 from 210ms -> 64ms. End-to-end throughput unaffected for steady loads.

Operational considerations and tradeoffs:
- Background warmup and prefetch cost CPU/GPU cycles and must be budgeted; for dense multi-tenant nodes we throttle or gate warmup by SLAs.
- Prefetching risks wasted work on incorrect routing predictions; we use weak signals and a small prefetch budget. Observed <3% wasted prefetch in tests.
- Persistent autotune caches increase disk/state size for model shards; we cap cache size and apply LRU.

Open questions / next steps:
- Longer-term: investigate ability to move autotune off the hot path entirely by performing candidate microbenchmarks during model training/offline pipeline and shipping tuned profiles.
- Explore enabling a tiny persistent hot-kernel service that shares warmed kernels across tenants on the same node with secure isolation.
- Evaluate paged-attention page-granularity tradeoffs: smaller tiles reduce copy latencies but increase metadata overhead; run a sweep across tile sizes for our most common long-context customers.
- Add lightweight in-runtime telemetry for alloc slow paths to detect fragmentation events and trigger background defragmentation.

Appendix: representative commands & scripts used
- workload driver (chat-burst): ./bench/drivers/chat_burst_driver --config experiments/chat_burst/short.json --runs 50
- nvtrace capture: nvprof --profile-from-start off --analysis-metrics -o traces/run1.nvtx ./runtime-bin ...
- kernel-selection logging enabled via env: RW_AUTOTUNE_LOG=1 RW_AUTOTUNE_CACHE_DIR=/var/tmp/atune_cache
- allocator debug: export RW_ALLOC_DEBUG=1; logs written to /var/log/rw_alloc_debug.log

Action items (owners):
- Persist cached autotune artifacts in shard metadata (Owen) — target: 2026-03-24
- Add async fused-op registration scaffolding (Priya) — target: 2026-03-31
- Implement simple route-hint prefetch heuristic and set default budget to 3 tiles (Ethan) — target: 2026-03-20
- Run production canary for combined mitigations on 2 low-traffic clusters (Maya) — target: 2026-04-07

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is deliberately experimental and contains raw numbers collected from lab nodes. Please review assumptions about prefetch budgets and proposed defaults closely; we need SRE signoff before turning on mitigations globally.

End of journal entry.
